summary:
Valle del Cauca stands under Colombia's national framework, among the more developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Facilities access is protected by Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali, within Valle del Cauca) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk), which bar exclusion from public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 4 April 2025 Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video circulated on 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police questioned local residents but made no arrest even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. These incidents occurred in Antioquia and elsewhere, not Valle del Cauca, but the bearing for a visitor to Valle del Cauca is national: lethal anti-trans violence has occurred in daylight, has been filmed, and has gone unpunished.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed actors. In Caquetá department, armed groups ran a 'social cleansing' campaign with flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets; a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night, and a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. The Guardian article offers no Valle del Cauca-specific finding; its bearing on Valle del Cauca is the pattern of territorial violence and displacement by armed actors.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Discrimination limits trans women in Colombia mainly to hairdressing or sex work, an economic constraint that shapes where trans people can be seen and how they are targeted.

A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration nationally in 2025, so the current framework rests on notary-based marker change, Constitutional Court jurisprudence and administrative decrees rather than a single consolidated statute.
